bib.title: Large Language Models on Graphs: A Comprehensive Survey
bib.venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering (TKDE) 2024 (arXiv v4, 20 Nov 2024; first posted Dec 2023)

read.skipped: Reference list (pages 16-20) and author biographies skimmed only; appendix tables 4-8 read in full.

question: How can large language models be used on graphs (pure, text-attributed, text-paired), and which techniques, datasets and open problems exist?
contributions: Categorization of graph scenarios: pure graphs, text-attributed graphs, text-paired graphs
Systematic review of techniques (LLM as Predictor, Encoder, Aligner)
Collection of benchmark datasets, open-source codebases and applications

results.claim: LLM-on-graph techniques split into three roles: LLM as Predictor, Encoder, Aligner, over three graph scenarios (pure, text-attributed, text-paired).
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: We then discuss detailed techniques for utilizing LLMs on graphs, including LLM as Predictor, LLM as Encoder, and LLM as Aligner

results.claim: LLMs answer easy pure-graph questions (connectivity, neighbor identification, size counting) but fail on cycle detection and Hamiltonian pathfinding.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: LLMs can answer easier questions such as connectivity, neighbor identification, and graph size counting but fail to answer more complex questions such as cycle detection and Hamiltonian pathfinding.

results.claim: Fine-tuning with a graph encoder gives drastic gains on substructure counting, max triplet sum, shortest path, bipartite matching.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: By encoding graphs into features, [41] demonstrates drastic performance improvement on problems including substructure counting, maximum triplet sum, shortest path, and bipartite matching.

results.claim: CoT helps on simpler graph problems (cycle detection, shortest path) but gains are inconsistent or vanish on Hamiltonian path and topological sorting.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: CoT-style reasoning can improve the performance on simpler problems, such as cycle detection and shortest path detection.

results.claim: Algorithmic Prompting did not show consistent improvement over heuristic reasoning.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: Their results, however, do not show consistent improvement over the heuristic reasoning approach.

results.claim: Linearized structure helps node classification mainly when node text is scarce.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: find that the structure information is beneficial when the textual information associated with the node is scarce

results.claim: Two-step training (train LLM on task, freeze, then train GNN) gives outstanding performance; LoRA alleviates overfitting.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: SimTeG [34] finds that the simple framework of first training the LLMs on the downstream task and then fixing the LLMs and training the GNNs can result in outstanding performance.

results.claim: Joint one-step LLM-GNN training suffers efficiency (few one-hop neighbors fit in memory) and local-minimum (LLM underfits) issues.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: Joint training LLMs and GNNs in a cascaded pipeline is convenient but may suffer from efficiency [67] (only support sampling a few one-hop neighbors regarding memory complexity) and local minimal [34] (LLM underfits the data) issues.

results.claim: Two-step training is costlier than one-step but gives better text representation quality.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: The two-step strategy can effectively alleviate the insufficient training of the LLM which contributes to higher text representation quality but is more computationally expensive and time-consuming than the one-step training strategy.

results.claim: LLM-GNN cascade inference is slow (neighbor sampling plus encoding each neighbor); distilling into a student LLM avoids neighbor sampling; distilling to smaller LM or MLP suggested.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: A potential solution is to distill the model into a much smaller LM or even an MLP.

results.claim: Pretrained GINs in reviewed molecule-text aligner works are small: five layers, 300 hidden dims; GNN scale may be a bottleneck.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: These pretrained GINs feature five layers and 300 hidden dimensions.

results.claim: GPT-3.5/4 may be less adept with SELFIES than SMILES.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: LLMs, such as GPT-3.5/4, may be less adept at using SELFIES compared to SMILES.

results.claim: Rule-based linearization breaks permutation invariance of molecular graphs; multiple string views of one molecule can improve sequence models.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: Rule-based linearization methods introduce inductive biases for sequence modeling, thereby breaking the permutation invariance assumption inherent in molecular graphs.

results.claim: Graph-empowered LLM defined by asymmetric multi-head attention over virtual structure tokens in each Transformer layer.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: Graph-Empowered LLMs are proposed. They have a shared philosophy of introducing virtual structure tokens

results.claim: No consensus on best graph representation in LLMs; needs balance of computation efficiency and information completeness.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: there has not been a consensus about the best practice in graph representation in LLMs

results.claim: Graph linearization length grows with graph size, hitting LLM max input length and time/memory cost.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: the length of the transferred sequence will increase significantly as the size of the graph increases

results.claim: Galactica reaches 120B parameters, pretrained on two million PubChem compounds.
results.setup: Survey statement about surveyed work, no new experiment
results.quote: Galactica [176] is a set of LLMs with a maximum of 120 billion parameters, which is pretrained on two million compounds from PubChem [181].

limits: Survey: no new experiments; all numbers are dataset statistics or model sizes, results are qualitative statements about cited work.
Authors concede no consensus on best graph representation in LLMs (Sec 4.4).
Authors note existing graph-empowered LLMs are mostly encoder-only and pretraining is mostly on homogeneous text-attributed networks (Sec 5.1.4).
Most reviewed molecule works use small GINs as proof of concept (Sec 6.2.2).
Coverage ends around late 2023 / 2024; later GraphRAG and graph-agent work is not covered.
practices: For pure-graph reasoning, combine heuristic, algorithmic and search-based reasoning rather than treating them as exclusive (Sec 4.4).
Use code-style graph descriptions (XML/JSON) with code LLMs as a zero-shot structure-aware sequence (Sec 5.1.4, proposed).
Use LLM-as-encoder: LLM text features feed a GNN; prefer two-step training (adapt LLM first, then fit GNN) with LoRA to avoid overfitting (Sec 5.2.1).
Distill LLM-GNN cascades into a pure LLM or MLP for fast inference (Sec 5.2.3, 5.2.4).
Align text and graph encoders with contrastive InfoNCE-style losses or iterative pseudo-label exchange (Sec 5.3).
For molecules, prefer SELFIES over SMILES for validity but note LLMs know SMILES better (Sec 6.1.1, 6.1.3).
Evaluate TAG tasks with Accuracy/Macro-F1/Micro-F1, MRR/NDCG/Hit; molecule classification with AUC, regression MAE/RMSE/R2, captioning BLEU (Sec 7.1).

terms.definition: graphs where nodes or edges are associated with semantically rich text information
graphs [that] have textual descriptions defined for the entire graph structure
serves LLM as the final component to output representations or predictions
LLMs are first utilized to encode the text associated with the nodes/edges; the feature vectors serve as input embeddings for GNNs
adopts LLMs as text-encoding components and aligns them with GNNs which serve as graph structure encoding components
makes no changes to the LLM architecture, but makes it be aware of graph structure by taking a graph token sequence as input
modifies the architecture of the LLM base model (i.e., Transformers) to conduct joint text and graph encoding
only fine-tunes the LLMs with supervision from the graph, no change to input or architecture
pseudo labels from one modality train the other iteratively (LTRN, GLEM)
cross-modality contrastive learning between LLM text embeddings and GNN graph embeddings
